Power & utilities · Tanzania

Power-line wayleaves in Tanzania: structures, vegetation and new routes

The Electricity Act requires a licensee to acquire a wayleave for its facilities. Owners on or bordering the wayleave must not interfere with it (s.37), and the licensee must “remove or trim trees or other high vegetation which may pose threat to the safe and reliable operation” of its facilities (s.36(3)). Tanzania’s grid is growing, with new 400 kV and 220 kV lines and cross-border interconnectors. We map structures and tall vegetation inside each wayleave band, so your maintenance and land teams know where to go first.

Request a proposal See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Under the line, between inspections

Transmission wayleaves cross farmland, bush and the edges of towns, and the land under a line changes between inspections. What changes decides where a maintenance crew, a wayleave officer or a valuer goes next.

“There are houses under the line.”

Houses, shops and outbuildings can go up inside the wayleave, especially where a line passes a village or a trading centre. Section 37(2) says owners on or bordering a wayleave shall not interfere with the licensee’s rights; a dated list shows where each structure stands and since when.

“The trees are growing into the wayleave.”

Section 36(3) puts the duty on the licensee: “remove or trim trees or other high vegetation which may pose threat to the safe and reliable operation” of its facilities. Knowing where tall vegetation stands lets crews go there first.

“A landowner wants the line moved.”

On a landowner’s application, EWURA may order the licensee to alter the position of a line or remove it (s.36(4)). The first questions are what stood where, and when it appeared.

“The valuation is disputed.”

Wayleave disputes reach the High Court: an interim injunction against demolishing a house pending trial of the encroachment and compensation issues ([2014] TZHC 2736), and a supplementary valuation upheld where the first assessment was in doubt ([2025] TZHC 3298, as summarised on TanzLII).

In July 2026 the Deputy Minister for Energy told utility managers in Mara region to identify every place where power lines pass over homes that are not yet connected, so that those households can be connected. A structure register of what stands under each line is where that list starts.

The law in Tanzania

The wayleave duties behind every line

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; our wayleave-law guide has the detail and the sources.

Instrument What it sets
Electricity Act, Cap. 131 R.E. 2023, s.36(1) Compulsory access to private property on written notice to the landowner and EWURA
Electricity Act, s.36(3) The licensee “shall remove or trim trees or other high vegetation which may pose threat to the safe and reliable operation of his facilities”
Electricity Act, s.36(4) On the landowner’s application, EWURA may order the licensee to alter the position of a line or remove it
Electricity Act, s.37 “The licensee shall acquire a wayleave for electricity facilities”; owners on or bordering it “shall not interfere”; the licensee compensates the property owner, with disputes settled as if the wayleave had been obtained under the Land Acquisition Act
Electricity Act, s.38 Compulsory acquisition through the Minister for lands, with EWURA’s consent
Electricity activities regulations, 2024 (GN 679 of 2024) A licence applicant shows a wayleave, or proof that the process of obtaining one has started (haki ya njia au uthibitisho wa kuanza mchakato)
Land Act, Cap. 113, ss.161, 166, 186–187 A wayleave runs with the land; compensation for trees, crops and buildings; removal orders for obstructions and encroachments on a public right of way

The wayleave itself is haki ya njia ya umeme, and a transmission line njia ya kusafirisha umeme. We found no statutory wayleave width by voltage, so each survey is measured against your own standard. Wayleave law in Tanzania

Structures under the line

A register of what stands in the wayleave, band by band

We buffer the line in its UTM zone, list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the line and its band, and cut the route into 500 m stretches. Each stretch is rated for encroachment density: high where more than five structures stand inside the widest band, medium for one to five, low for none. It is a count rule that tells your wayleave officers where to go first, not a safety rating.

Towers and substations are the utility’s own assets and stay out of the register. After the baseline, the line is re-surveyed on a schedule agreed with you: new and removed structures are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and your team receives a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. Fresh digging and new tracks near towers and underground cable routes are flagged the same way.

Each report names the imagery and its capture date, so the register can be read against the date the wayleave was acquired or a valuation was approved.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, distance to the line, band, chainage and coordinates
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between surveys, with before-and-after views
  • Tall vegetation inside the wayleave, and where it was cleared or regrew
  • Fire-hotspot notices near lines and substations
  • A PDF report in English, with GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Vegetation in the wayleave

Where tall vegetation stands, and where it came back

Section 36(3) makes vegetation a standing duty, and the question every maintenance plan starts from is where the tall vegetation is. We map it inside each wayleave band from drone elevation models where they are flown and from open canopy-height data elsewhere, and compare vegetation cover between dates from Copernicus Sentinel imagery to show where the wayleave was cleared and where it has regrown.

In the dry season, bush fires can run through a wayleave. We send notices of satellite-detected fire hotspots near your lines and substations and map the burnt area afterwards, so crews can check towers and conductors that were near a fire.

The limits

  • Larger patches of vegetation, not individual trees
  • Not a measured clearance to conductors, and not a species survey
  • Open canopy-height data is older in places; drone surveys give the current picture
  • Fires that are small, short-lived or under cloud can be missed; it is not an early-warning service
  • Copernicus Sentinel and NASA FIRMS data are credited as their licences require

New lines and interconnectors

Route options and a baseline before the valuation

Tanzania reported installed generating capacity of 4,646 MW against a peak demand of 2,271 MW in August 2026, with agreements to sell power to Zambia and to trade with Kenya. Moving that power takes new lines.

A 345 km 400 kV line was reported 99 per cent complete in August 2026. A World Bank-financed programme approved in 2018 covers about 620 km of 400 kV double-circuit line in the south-west, towards the Zambian border, and a 128 km 220 kV line with a new substation is in preparation in the south. At regional level, the Eastern Africa Power Pool’s Council of Ministers resolved in July 2026 to speed up the common power market.

Every new line starts with route options. We count the structures along each alternative alignment within the wayleave bands, so the route and land teams can compare options on the land they would affect, alongside engineering and environmental criteria. Once the route is chosen, a dated baseline before the valuation, and another on the cut-off date, show what stood in the wayleave and what appeared in between.

During construction

Dated drone orthophotos and elevation models, compared between visits, show tower-site earthworks and access tracks as they are built, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. Between drone visits, dated satellite scenes show new access roads and cleared ground along the route.

Substations and switching stations

Around the fence line

Around substations, the question is what is being built against the fence and on the access road. We map new structures, cleared ground and new tracks in a ring around each site between dates. Fence lines and gates are too thin to detect on satellite imagery, so a reviewer checks them on drone imagery where it is flown.

Drone work near lines and substations

Lines, towers and substations are structures under GN 268 of 2026, so flights keep 50 m from them and from people not under the operator’s control unless TCAA approves closer work (reg 30). GN 268 sets no live-line distance: your own safety rules decide it. Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals, and every drone proposal names the company that will fly.

Drone law in Tanzania

How it works

From line file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the line route or tower coordinates, the voltage, the regions and the wayleave widths from your standard, and what the record is for. We agree the bands, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures, vegetation and ground change are mapped along the whole line from dated satellite imagery, open building and canopy datasets, or the imagery you hold.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the spans that need detail, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result; each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the report goes to the contacts you name with the GIS layers.

Public procuring entities in Tanzania, state utilities among them, procure through NeST, the national e-procurement system (Public Procurement Act, 2023, s.73). See working with AfriScan in Tanzania and the global power and utilities page.

Frequently asked questions

Which wayleave widths do you use?

The ones in your own standard for each voltage, or the wayleave polygons you have acquired. We found no statutory wayleave width by voltage in the Electricity Act or the regulations we read, so we measure against the widths you give us, with up to six bands in one survey, and report each structure’s distance to the line.

Can you measure clearance to the conductors?

No. We map where tall vegetation stands inside the wayleave, from drone elevation models where flown and from open canopy-height data, and where vegetation has been cleared or has regrown between dates. That tells your maintenance teams where to trim first under s.36(3). It is not a measured clearance to the conductors, and open canopy-height data is older in places, so a drone survey gives the current picture.

Can the register help with a landowner's application to move a line?

It can show what stood inside the wayleave on each survey date, and roughly when a structure first appeared, which is what an application under s.36(4) or a compensation dispute usually turns on. Whether EWURA orders a line moved, and what is payable, is for EWURA, the valuers and the courts.

Can you list homes under our lines that are not yet connected?

We can list the structures under and near a line, with their distances and coordinates. Whether a house is connected to the grid is not visible from above, so the register is a starting list for your connection teams, not a connection survey.

Do you watch for fires near our lines?

We send notices of satellite-detected fire hotspots near your lines and substations, from NASA FIRMS data, and map the burnt area afterwards. It is not an emergency or early-warning service, and small, short-lived or cloud-covered fires can be missed.

How close can a drone fly to a live line?

GN 268 of 2026 sets no live-line distance, so the utility’s own safety rules decide it. Lines, towers and substations are structures, so the regulations’ 50 m rule applies unless TCAA approves closer work. Drone surveys are subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires.

Send us the line and its wayleave widths

The line route or tower coordinates (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the voltage, the regions it crosses and the wayleave widths from your own standard. Tell us whether the record is for maintenance, a wayleave dispute, a new route or a valuation. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
